title: The Bengazi club and the Dunbar Hotel in Washington
summary: Ben takes Leeman to the black Bengazi nightclub in Washington, with Sonny Wright and Teddy Sturgis, and they stay at the Dunbar Hotel where Ben protects the only white guest.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: We had so much in common that we damn near self destructed. So on with the Ben Gazi incident. About the last of '47 or early '48, Ben asked me if I wanted to go to Washington, he was going to the Ben Gazi nightclub, it was a black club in the black district in Washington, D.C. The band was Sonny Wright on piano -- and oh, he was a lovely piano player, he made so many records that Teddy Wilson got credit for behind Billie Holiday, they sounded a great deal alike -- and Teddy Sturgis on bass.

And I took the saddle with me, as I discussed, and he checked us into the Dunbar Hotel, it was an all black clientele, and I was told at that time that it was the largest hotel in the world, up to that time. And I was the only white person to stay there -- there were hundreds of blacks. And Ben told the management and anyone concerned that I was to be looked out for, not to have anyone bother me, and he was looking out for my safety. And this was a reversal of the racial difficulties blacks suffered.

After checking in the hotel -- and they were a gang of lovely people in Washington, D.C., so many, and of course, the black society was in Washington, D.C. for one thing, and Ben's first wife came from there. And he was wined and dined
by all the professors at the university; a great deal of them lived there, and ...

I would just like to interject here and mention -- excuse me, Cliff -- that the university to be mentioned is Howard University, which is a very prestigous, was then and still is a very prestigous black university. So that's just for the record.
Hey, we didn't mention, also, that Ben's wife was from Washington, D.C. -- she was a lawyer, an attorney, which really put him into the black society of Washington, D.C. Now please carry on.
